chapter.name: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice

questions.q: The chapter sorts our preferences into needs and wants. Which of these does it give as a need?
questions.a: Shelter

questions.q: The chapter says resources can be natural or human-made. Which of these is a human-made resource?
questions.a: Capital

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four factors of production named in the chapter?
questions.a: Demand

questions.q: A gram panchayat owns one empty plot of land. Some villagers want a playground on it, some want a health centre and some want a row of shops. The plot is big enough for only one of these. Which idea from the chapter explains why the panchayat must choose?
questions.a: Resources are limited in quantity and can be put to many alternative uses.
o: Resources are limited in quantity and can be put to many alternative uses.
Wants stay the same over time, so one choice settles them for ever.
Land is a human-made resource, so it can be made again when needed.
A resource can have only one use, so the plot must go to the oldest demand.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. People's wants keep changing over their lives. II. Only natural resources such as water and coal are limited; human-made resources such as capital and technology are not. III. Not just households but whole economies have to decide how to use their scarce resources. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: How does the chapter define a market? Name the two forms a market can take.
questions.a: A market is a place where buying and selling of products and services takes place. It can be a physical market or a virtual one on the internet.
s: Defines a market as a place where products and services are bought and sold
Names the two forms: a physical market and a virtual market on the internet

questions.q: True or False: According to the chapter, both natural and human-made resources are limited in quantity. Give a reason with one example of each kind.
questions.a: True. The chapter says both natural resources (such as water and coal) and human-made resources (such as capital and technology) are limited in quantity, so they must be used carefully among their many uses.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: both kinds are limited, with one natural example (water or coal) and one human-made example (capital or technology)

questions.q: A school hostel buys these things in one month: drinking water, a music system, food grains and a holiday trip for the staff. (a) Sort the four into needs and wants. (b) Give the reason for putting food grains where you put them.
questions.a: (a) Needs: drinking water and food grains. Wants: the music system and the holiday trip. (b) Food grains are food, one of the essentials (food, water and shelter) that the chapter calls needs; a music system or a holiday is a comfort, like the gadgets and vacations the chapter calls wants.
s: (a) Needs: drinking water, food grains; wants: music system, holiday trip
(b) Food grains are food, an essential the chapter lists as a need, not a comfort or luxury

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Name any two needs the chapter lists. (b) Name any two wants the chapter lists. (c) Name the two kinds of resources by where they come from, with one example of each.
questions.a: (a) Any two of food, water and shelter. (b) Any two of gadgets, vacations and luxury items. (c) Natural resources, such as water or coal, and human-made resources, such as capital or technology.
s: (a) Any two of food, water, shelter
(b) Any two of gadgets, vacations, luxury items
(c) Natural (water or coal) and human-made (capital or technology)

questions.q: Kavya says, 'If a factory gets enough capital and technology, it can make everything people want, and then there will be no scarcity.' Examine her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Kavya is wrong. First, the chapter says human wants are unlimited and keep changing, so even a large output never satisfies all of them; new wants appear. Second, capital and technology are human-made resources, and the chapter says human-made resources are also limited in quantity. Third, the factory also needs natural resources such as water and coal, which are limited and have other uses. So scarcity, the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources, remains.
s: Verdict that the claim is wrong, because wants are unlimited and keep changing
Capital and technology are themselves limited human-made resources
Natural resources needed for production are also limited and have alternative uses, so scarcity remains

questions.q: Bhola Pottery in Khurja uses clay dug from a nearby field, water from a borewell, an electric kiln and six potters. Last month it had enough clay for either 2,000 flower pots or 1,200 water pitchers, not both. (a) Name the factor of production that the kiln and the potters each represent. (b) Which two inputs are natural resources? (c) Give one alternative use of the borewell water outside the workshop. (d) Explain, using the idea of scarcity, why the pottery had to choose between pots and pitchers.
questions.a: (a) The kiln is capital; the potters are labour. (b) The clay and the borewell water are natural resources. (c) The water could be used for drinking, for washing or for watering crops in the field. (d) The clay is limited in quantity and has alternative uses, while customers want both pots and pitchers; because the clay cannot meet both wants, the pottery must choose one use and give up the other.
s: (a) Kiln = capital; potters = labour
(b) Clay and water are the natural resources
(c) One sensible alternative use of the water, such as drinking or irrigating crops
(d) Clay is limited and has alternative uses while wants exceed it, so one use must be chosen and the other given up

questions.q: In a dry summer, the groundwater of a coastal town can supply 30 lakh litres a day. Households ask for 18 lakh litres for drinking, cooking and washing, a cold-drink bottling plant asks for 10 lakh litres, and a new water park asks for 6 lakh litres. (i) Show by calculation that the town cannot meet all three demands. (ii) Which demand is for a need and which is for a want? (iii) Explain why this is an economic problem, using the chapter's idea of scarcity. (iv) Recommend which demand the town should cut or reduce, and justify your choice by naming what is given up.
questions.a: (i) 18 + 10 + 6 = 34 lakh litres are asked for, but only 30 lakh are available, a shortfall of 4 lakh litres. (ii) The household demand is for needs (water for drinking and cooking is an essential); the water park is for a want (entertainment). The bottling plant makes a product people want, not an essential. (iii) Water is a natural resource that is limited in quantity and has alternative uses, while the wants placed on it are larger, so the town must choose how to use it. (iv) A sound choice: give households their full 18 lakh litres first; then closing the water park for the summer frees 6 lakh, so 18 + 10 = 28 lakh fits within 30 lakh with 2 lakh to spare. What is given up is the water park's entertainment (and its earnings). Another justified choice, such as cutting the bottling plant to 6 lakh litres, earns full marks if it names what is given up and keeps households supplied.
s: (i) Total 34 lakh litres against 30 lakh available: short by 4 lakh
(ii) Households = need; water park = want (bottling plant not an essential)
(iii) Water is limited and has alternative uses while wants exceed it: scarcity forces a choice
(iv) A recommendation that keeps household needs met and fits within 30 lakh litres
(iv) Names what is given up (the opportunity cost) of the choice

questions.q: What does the chapter call the value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen?
questions.a: Opportunity cost

questions.q: In Fig. 8.3, the farmer's Production Possibility Curve, what does the x-axis show?
questions.a: The quantity of barley grown, in kg
o: The quantity of barley grown, in kg
The quantity of wheat grown, in kg
The area of land used, in acres
The price of barley, in rupees

questions.q: In the farmer's table of combinations, combination D has 75 kg of barley. How much wheat goes with it?
questions.a: 40 kg

questions.q: What do all the points on a Production Possibility Curve show, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The maximum output that can be produced through efficient use of resources, avoiding wastage
o: The maximum output that can be produced through efficient use of resources, avoiding wastage
The output produced when only half of the resources are used
The prices at which the two goods are sold in the market
The quantities of the two goods that people want to buy

questions.q: Match each choice with the opportunity cost it carries. 1. A farmer uses her only field for wheat 2. A government spends its funds on highways 3. A firm uses its steel for aircraft parts 4. A student spends his pocket money on snacks. a. The new pair of shoes he was saving for b. The hospitals that could have been built c. The barley that could have grown there d. The refrigerators that could have been made

A pottery workshop can make these daily combinations of cups and plates when all its potters, clay and kilns are used: P (0 cups, 80 plates), Q (15, 72), R (30, 56), S (45, 32), T (60, 0). Which of these daily outputs can the workshop NOT produce with its resources?
questions.a: 30 cups and 70 plates, because with 30 cups the most it can make is 56 plates
o: 30 cups and 70 plates, because with 30 cups the most it can make is 56 plates
45 cups and 30 plates, because it is less than combination S
15 cups and 72 plates, because it uses every resource
60 cups and no plates, because it makes no plates at all

questions.q: Assertion (A): The farmer's Production Possibility Curve slopes downward from A to E. Reason (R): With limited land, water and labour, growing more barley means some wheat must be given up. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Define opportunity cost, and give the chapter's farmer example of it.
questions.a: Opportunity cost is the value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen. When the farmer grows more barley on her limited land, some wheat must be given up; that wheat is the opportunity cost of growing barley.
s: Definition: the value of what is given up when a choice is made
Example: the wheat given up to grow more barley

questions.q: True or False: In the farmer's table, combination E shows the farmer growing only wheat. Correct the statement if it is wrong.
questions.a: False. Combination E is 100 kg of barley and 0 kg of wheat, so the farmer grows only barley there. It is combination A (0 kg barley, 100 kg wheat) that shows only wheat.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: E is 100 kg barley and no wheat; A (0 barley, 100 wheat) is the only-wheat combination

questions.q: Use the tailoring unit's weekly combinations (shirts, kurtas): P (0, 60), Q (20, 50), R (40, 30), S (60, 0). (a) How many kurtas are given up for the first 20 shirts (P to Q)? (b) How many kurtas are given up for the last 20 shirts (R to S)? (c) What happens to the opportunity cost of shirts as the unit makes more of them?
questions.a: (a) 60 - 50 = 10 kurtas. (b) 30 - 0 = 30 kurtas. (c) It rises: each extra batch of 20 shirts costs more kurtas (10, then 20, then 30).
s: (a) 10 kurtas
(b) 30 kurtas
(c) The opportunity cost rises with each extra batch of shirts (10, 20, 30 kurtas)

questions.q: A village cooperative can use all its land to grow rice and cotton in these combinations (in tonnes of rice, tonnes of cotton): A (0, 48), B (15, 44), C (30, 36), D (45, 22), E (60, 0). Answer each part in one line. (i) What is the most cotton it can grow if it grows no rice? (ii) How much cotton goes with 30 tonnes of rice? (iii) How much cotton is given up when it moves from B to C? (iv) What is that given-up cotton called? (v) Name the curve these combinations make when plotted.
questions.a: (i) 48 tonnes. (ii) 36 tonnes (combination C). (iii) 44 - 36 = 8 tonnes. (iv) The opportunity cost of the extra 15 tonnes of rice. (v) The Production Possibility Curve (PPC).
s: (i) 48 tonnes
(ii) 36 tonnes
(iii) 8 tonnes
(iv) Opportunity cost of the extra rice
(v) Production Possibility Curve

questions.q: Read the case and answer. A small electronics factory in Noida can assemble these weekly combinations of phones and tablets when all its workers and machines are used: P (0 phones, 400 tablets), Q (300, 350), R (600, 250), S (900, 100), T (1,200, 0). Last week it made 600 phones and only 200 tablets because one assembly line stood idle for two days. The firm earns Rs 2,000 on each phone and Rs 5,000 on each tablet. A shop chain has now asked for 900 phones a week. (a) How many tablets were lost last week, and why is the point (600, 200) not on the curve? (b) What is the opportunity cost, in tablets, of moving from R to S? (c) Find the weekly earnings at R and at S. (d) Should the firm produce at R or at S? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) At 600 phones the curve allows 250 tablets, so 250 - 200 = 50 tablets were lost; the point is inside the curve (below the maximum the curve allows) because resources (the idle line) were wasted, while points on the PPC show maximum output through efficient use. (b) 250 - 100 = 150 tablets. (c) R: 600 x 2,000 + 250 x 5,000 = Rs 24,50,000. S: 900 x 2,000 + 100 x 5,000 = Rs 23,00,000. (d) R earns Rs 1,50,000 more a week, so on earnings alone R is better; giving up 150 tablets to make 300 more phones costs more than it brings. S is defensible only if the firm values the shop chain's order (a steady customer) above that Rs 1.5 lakh. Either choice earns the mark if it uses the figures and names what is given up.
s: (a) 50 tablets lost; the point is inside the curve (below the maximum it allows) because the idle line wasted resources
(b) 150 tablets
(c) R = Rs 24.5 lakh, S = Rs 23 lakh
(d) A decision justified with the Rs 1.5 lakh difference and what is given up

questions.q: The word Economics comes from the Greek oikonomia, made of oikos and nemein. What is nemein best translated as?
questions.a: Management

questions.q: The chapter says the Economic Survey of India acts as a blueprint for which document?
questions.a: The upcoming Union Budget

questions.q: Families divide their money among essential items, non-essential items and savings. Which of these does the chapter list as a non-essential item?
questions.a: Jewellery

questions.q: Dr Fernandes studies economic trends and teaches economics at a university. Which area of an economist's work, shown in Fig. 8.4, is this?
questions.a: Research and education

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Data are facts and statistics collected together for reference or analysis. II. Enterprises study market trends and new innovations to serve customers better and maximise profits. III. Economists decide what each family must buy, so families need not make their own choices. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Economic Survey is useful to ordinary citizens, not only to policymakers. Reason (R): The Survey is written only for policymakers, in technical language that citizens cannot follow. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What does the discipline of Economics deal with, according to the chapter? Name any two economic entities whose interaction it explains.
questions.a: Economics deals with how choices are made by optimising the use of limited resources to satisfy needs and wants. It explains how economic entities such as consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions interact (any two).
s: Economics deals with making choices by optimising the use of limited resources to satisfy needs and wants
Any two of consumers, producers, governments, financial institutions

questions.q: True or False: The Economic Survey of India is brought out once every year. Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter calls the Economic Survey an important annual document; it is prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented in Parliament before the Union Budget, reviewing the economy's performance during the past year.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: it is an annual document, prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented before each Union Budget, reviewing the past year

questions.q: Salma runs a tea stall near a bus stand and must decide how much milk to buy each morning. (a) Which kind of economic entity is Salma? (b) Explain how she could use data rather than guesswork to make this decision.
questions.a: (a) She is a producer (a small enterprise selling tea). (b) She could note the number of cups sold each day for a few weeks, find the usual daily sale (and busier days), and buy milk to match it, so that less milk is wasted and fewer customers are turned away; the chapter says good decisions rely on data and analysis, not guesswork.
s: (a) A producer or enterprise
(b) Records past daily sales and buys milk to match them, instead of guessing

questions.q: Rohit says, 'Economics is only about how prices are set in the market.' How far is he right? Answer with the chapter's own examples.
questions.a: Rohit is only partly right. How prices are determined in the market is one of the things economics studies. But the chapter lists much more: how people work and earn wages, how wealth and resources are distributed, how education and technology drive investment, and how government policies and trade affect employment. At its core, economics is about how consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions make choices with limited resources, not only about prices.
s: Partly right: price-setting is one topic economics studies
Names at least two other topics from the chapter (wages, distribution of wealth, investment, policy and employment)
Economics is about choices with limited resources by all economic entities, so the claim is too narrow

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Which ministry prepares the Economic Survey of India? (b) Name any two sectors or areas of the economy it analyses. (c) Give one way it helps citizens.
questions.a: (a) The Ministry of Finance. (b) Any two of agriculture, industry, services, employment, inflation, education, health and infrastructure. (c) It explains economic data in a clear manner, so people understand how the economy is performing and what steps the government may take.
s: (a) Ministry of Finance
(b) Any two sectors or areas named in the chapter
(c) It explains economic data clearly so citizens understand the economy's performance

questions.q: Read the case and answer. Ward 14 of a municipal corporation in Nashik has money for only one project this year. Instead of guessing, the ward committee carried out a survey of 400 households. 260 households said the nearest doctor is more than 5 km away, 90 said no bus runs from their lane to the main market, and 50 said they had no problem. The committee will choose between opening a primary health centre and starting a new bus route. (a) What is a survey, as the chapter defines it? (b) What percentage of households reported that the doctor is too far? (c) Which project does the survey data support, and what is the opportunity cost of choosing it? (d) Why is a decision based on this survey better than a guess?
questions.a: (a) A survey is a systematic method for collecting and analysing data about the economic conditions and behaviours of a population. (b) 260 / 400 x 100 = 65%. (c) The primary health centre, since 65% of households report that problem against 22.5% (90 of 400) for the bus route; the opportunity cost is the bus route given up this year. (d) The chapter says good decisions rely on data and analysis, not guesswork; the survey shows which problem affects the most people, so the limited money goes where it helps most.
s: (a) A systematic method of collecting and analysing data on economic conditions and behaviours
(c) Primary health centre; opportunity cost = the bus route given up
(d) Good decisions rely on data, not guesswork; it shows which problem affects most households

questions.q: Which crops does the chapter give as examples of drought-resistant crops?
questions.a: Millets and pulses

questions.q: What does labour-intensive production mean, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: Using more workers and less machinery
o: Using more workers and less machinery
Using more machines and technology and fewer workers
Using more land and less capital
Using only family members as workers

questions.q: A toy company has already decided to make toy cars of one design on its machines. Now it must decide whether to sell them mainly to low-income families at a low price or to high-income buyers at a high price. Which key question of economics is it answering now?
questions.a: For whom to produce
o: What the opportunity cost of the toy cars is

questions.q: Assertion (A): A garment manufacturer making customised, designer clothes relies on skilled labour. Reason (R): Advanced technology encourages the use of machines. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements about choosing a production technique. I. If machines are expensive, a firm will rely more on machines. II. Government laws, such as labour laws or incentives for machinery, can influence the choice. III. Limited technology leads to manual production. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: Match each type of shoe with what the chapter says it is made for. 1. School shoes 2. Office-wear shoes 3. Sports shoes 4. Casual shoes or slippers. a. Grip, flexibility and support, using special rubber soles and light materials b. Daily use by people, comfortable yet affordable c. Simple design, durable and affordable, for students d. Comfort, formal appearance and quality, often leather
Name the three key questions that the discipline of economics seeks to address, and state what gives rise to them.
questions.a: The three key questions are what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. They arise from the mismatch between unlimited wants and limited resources.
s: Names all three: what, how and for whom to produce
They arise from the mismatch between unlimited wants and limited resources

questions.q: True or False: Agriculture and handicrafts usually rely more on machinery than on labour. Correct the statement if it is wrong.
questions.a: False. The chapter says agriculture and handicrafts usually rely more on labour, while industries such as steel and automobile manufacturing depend more on machinery.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: agriculture and handicrafts rely more on labour; steel and automobile industries rely more on machinery

questions.q: A steel plant in Bhilai runs blast furnaces with a few hundred workers, while a handloom unit in Pochampally employs many weavers who make each sari with its own design. (a) Name the production method each one uses. (b) Give one reason from the chapter for the difference.
questions.a: (a) The steel plant is capital-intensive; the handloom unit is labour-intensive. (b) Any one: the nature of the product (steel is made in bulk and depends on machinery, while each designed sari needs skilled hands), or the technology available, or the relative cost of machines and labour.
s: (a) Steel plant capital-intensive; handloom unit labour-intensive
(b) One correct reason, such as the nature of the product (mass output vs customised design)

questions.q: The manager of a mobile phone company says, 'We will make only one expensive model and sell it to everyone, because every buyer wants the best phone.' Examine the claim using the chapter's idea of 'for whom to produce'.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. First, the chapter says people have different needs, income levels, tastes and lifestyles, so one expensive model will not suit buyers with low purchasing power. Second, producers decide which group of consumers to serve, as shoe makers make different shoes for students, office-goers and athletes; a phone firm likewise needs models for different groups. Third, producers should study what consumers like, how much money they have and how much demand there is, so that limited resources are used well and not wasted on phones few can buy.
s: Verdict: wrong, since buyers differ in needs, income, tastes and lifestyles
Producers choose the group they serve and make different products for different groups (as with shoes)
Studying likes, income and demand stops limited resources being wasted

questions.q: A furniture firm in Saharanpur makes two products: wooden doors hand-carved to each customer's design, and plain school desks that the state orders 5,000 at a time. Workers are cheap and easy to find locally, machines have to be imported at a high price, but the state now offers an incentive for buying machinery. (i) Which method should the firm use for the carved doors, and why? (ii) Which facts in the case pull the desks towards labour-intensive production? (iii) Which facts pull the desks towards machines? (iv) How could the government incentive change the decision? (v) Recommend one method for the desks and justify it.
questions.a: (i) Labour-intensive: customised or designer products need skilled labour. (ii) Labour is cheap and easily available, and machines are expensive, so the chapter says the firm would rely more on labour. (iii) The desks are plain and mass-produced in large orders, which the chapter says suit machines. (iv) The incentive lowers the cost of machines; the chapter says government laws and incentives for machinery influence the choice, and when machines become affordable a firm may shift to automation. (v) A justified recommendation: machines for the desks, since large identical orders suit machines and the incentive reduces their cost; or labour if the firm shows labour is still cheaper overall. The answer must weigh at least one fact from each side.
s: (i) Labour-intensive for carved doors, because customised products need skilled labour
(ii) Cheap, easily available labour and costly machines pull towards labour
(iii) Plain, mass-produced desks in large orders suit machines
(iv) The incentive makes machines more affordable, which can shift the firm to automation
(v) A recommendation for the desks that weighs facts from both sides

questions.q: Read the case and answer. A bicycle maker in Ludhiana surveyed 600 likely buyers before planning next year's production. 300 were school students who can spend about Rs 5,000 on a bicycle, 180 were office commuters who can spend about Rs 10,000, and 120 were sports riders who can spend about Rs 25,000. The firm has workers and machines for only two product lines, and each line can supply its whole group. (a) Which key economic question is the survey helping the firm answer? (b) What percentage of the buyers surveyed are school students? (c) Find the total sales value of each group if the firm supplies it. (d) Which two lines should the firm choose? Justify using your figures and say what is given up.
questions.a: (a) For whom to produce (which group of consumers to serve). (b) 300 / 600 x 100 = 50%. (c) Students: 300 x 5,000 = Rs 15 lakh; commuters: 180 x 10,000 = Rs 18 lakh; sports riders: 120 x 25,000 = Rs 30 lakh. (d) On sales value, sports riders and commuters give Rs 48 lakh, against Rs 45 lakh for sports and students or Rs 33 lakh for students and commuters, so sports and commuters is the strongest choice; the student market (Rs 15 lakh, half the buyers) is given up. A choice that keeps the student line because it is the largest group earns the mark if it uses the figures and names the Rs 3 lakh given up.
s: (a) For whom to produce
(c) Rs 15 lakh, Rs 18 lakh and Rs 30 lakh
(d) A choice of two lines justified with the totals, naming what is given up

questions.q: A solar-lamp company has money for only one plan next year. Plan X: make 20,000 basic lamps on an automated line and sell them at Rs 400 each to village families without electricity. Plan Y: have artisans hand-finish 2,000 designer lamps and sell them at Rs 3,500 each to city homes. (a) Find the sales value of each plan. (b) State how each plan answers the questions 'how to produce' and 'for whom to produce'. (c) Using your figures, which plan should the company choose, and what is the opportunity cost of that choice?
questions.a: (a) Plan X: 20,000 x 400 = Rs 80,00,000 (Rs 80 lakh). Plan Y: 2,000 x 3,500 = Rs 70,00,000 (Rs 70 lakh). (b) Plan X is capital-intensive (an automated line) and serves low-income village families; Plan Y is labour-intensive (artisans) and serves high-income city buyers. (c) On sales value Plan X is better by Rs 10 lakh; its opportunity cost is Plan Y given up, that is, the Rs 70 lakh of designer-lamp sales and the city buyers it would have served.
s: (a) X = Rs 80 lakh, Y = Rs 70 lakh
(b) X capital-intensive for low-income village families; Y labour-intensive for high-income city buyers
(c) Plan X (Rs 10 lakh more); opportunity cost = Plan Y's Rs 70 lakh sales and its buyers

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as an example of a planned economy?
questions.a: Cuba

questions.q: Public goods are available to all without anyone being excluded. Which of these is a public good, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Police services

questions.q: In the imaginary country of Tarvia, demand and supply decide what and how much is produced, most shops and factories belong to individuals and private companies, and the government keeps law and order without fixing prices. Which economic system does Tarvia have?
questions.a: A market economy
o: A mixed economy run by a planning commission
A state-led economy with licences and permits

questions.q: Which statement best describes the effect of the reforms India introduced from 1991, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: India shifted towards a more market-oriented system while still keeping an important role for the government.
o: India shifted towards a more market-oriented system while still keeping an important role for the government.
India became a pure market economy in which the government plays no part.
India moved to a planned economy with more licences and permits.
India closed its public sector so that only private firms remained.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a market economy, the government controls prices and production. Reason (R): In a market economy, the ownership of factories, shops and land largely rests with individuals and private companies. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: In a country, large public sector companies compete with private firms, the government sets rules for fair competition and runs welfare programmes, and businesses work to make a profit. Which conclusion fits the chapter?
questions.a: It is a mixed economy, like most economies in reality.
o: It is a mixed economy, like most economies in reality.
It is a planned economy, because public sector companies exist.
It is a market economy, because private firms make profits.
It cannot work, because the government and private firms cannot compete.

questions.q: State any two features of a planned economy, and name one country the chapter gives as an example.
questions.a: Any two: a central planning authority of the government decides what, how and for whom to produce and at what prices; the government owns most resources such as land, factories, banks and transport; enterprises follow the authority's targets and need strict permits and licences. Example: the former Soviet Union, North Korea or Cuba.
s: Any two correct features of a planned economy
One example: former Soviet Union, North Korea or Cuba

questions.q: True or False: In the decades after Independence, India followed a pure market economy. Correct the statement if it is wrong.
questions.a: False. In the decades after Independence India followed a more state-led approach similar to a planned economy: the government controlled industries and regulated production through licences and permits, and the public sector dominated banking, transport and heavy industries.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: India followed a state-led approach similar to a planned economy, with licences, permits and a large public sector

questions.q: Compare a planned economy and a market economy on (a) who decides what is produced, (b) how many enterprises compete, and (c) what this means for quality and innovation.
questions.a: (a) In a planned economy a central planning authority decides; in a market economy the forces of demand and supply decide. (b) In a planned economy strict permits and licences keep many enterprises out and restrict competition; in a market economy many producers offer similar products. (c) So a planned economy gives enterprises little motivation to improve quality or innovate, while competition in a market economy encourages better quality, lower prices and innovation.
s: (a) Central planning authority vs demand and supply
(b) Permits and licences restrict competition vs many producers of similar products
(c) Little motivation to improve or innovate vs better quality, lower prices and innovation

questions.q: A town has a public park, a cinema hall, street lights on its roads and a private coaching centre. (a) Identify the two public goods in this list. (b) Using the chapter's definition, explain why one of them is a public good. (c) Explain why the other two are not public goods. (d) Name the side of a mixed economy, in Fig. 8.8, that provides public goods, and give one other role of that side shown in the figure.
questions.a: (a) The public park and the street lights. (b) Street lights are available to everyone using the road, and one person's use does not stop others from using them, which is the chapter's definition of a public good. (c) A cinema hall and a coaching centre let in only those who pay for a ticket or a fee, so others can be excluded. (d) The government; another role shown is any one of welfare programmes, fair competition rules, consumer protection or transparency.
s: (a) Park and street lights
(b) Available to all, and one person's use does not prevent others' use
(c) The cinema and coaching centre exclude those who do not pay
(d) Government; one other role from Fig. 8.8 (welfare, fair competition rules, consumer protection, transparency)

questions.q: In a planned economy of the kind the chapter describes, a factory invents a cheaper and better water pump that many farmers want. Explain why the factory may still be unable to make and sell many more pumps.
questions.a: First, enterprises in a planned economy follow the central planning authority's targets rather than market demand, so the factory produces the number it is told to, however many farmers want the pump. Second, production needs strict permits and licences from the government, so it cannot simply expand or set its own prices. Third, because competition is restricted, the system rewards meeting targets rather than better products, which is why the chapter says there is little motivation to improve quality or innovate.
s: Enterprises follow the central authority's targets, not market demand
Strict permits and licences stop the factory expanding output or setting prices on its own
Restricted competition leaves little reward or motivation for better products

questions.q: Read about three imaginary countries. Country P: banks, railways and almost all land belong to the state, and a firm needs a government licence even to make more bicycles. Country Q: individuals and private companies own nearly all shops, land and banks, and the government, like a referee in a football match, only makes sure the rules are followed. Country R: its system is described as similar to Germany's and to China's after 1978; private firms and the government both make important economic choices, and the government regulates the private firms. (i) Name the system of P and give one clue. (ii) Name the system of Q and give one clue. (iii) Name the system of R and give one clue. (iv) In which country would the price of a bicycle most likely be fixed by the government? Why? (v) Country Q also runs public parks and police services from taxes. Does this make Q a planned economy? Explain.
questions.a: (i) Planned economy: the state owns most resources such as land and banks, and production needs government licences. (ii) Market economy: ownership is mainly private, and the government acts like a referee without controlling prices or production. (iii) Mixed economy: it is like Germany and China (post-1978), and the private sector and the government coexist, with the private players regulated by the government. (iv) P, because in a planned economy a central planning authority decides what is produced and at what prices. (v) No. The chapter says governments play an important role even in market economies, and the role of the government in a market economy is to provide public goods such as parks and police services; decisions on what and how much to produce are still made mainly by demand and supply, so Q remains a market economy.
s: (i) P = planned, with a correct clue (state ownership or licences)
(ii) Q = market, with a correct clue (private ownership or referee role)
(iii) R = mixed, with a correct clue (like Germany or China post-1978, government and private sector coexist)
(iv) P, because the central planning authority fixes prices
(v) No: even market economies have a government role, including providing public goods; production is still decided mainly by demand and supply

questions.q: Read the case and answer. In the hill town of Kotagiri, the 40 km of roads have few working lights. A private company offers to put up and run lights only on the 2 km main market road, charging each of the 120 shops on it Rs 300 a month. The residential lanes would stay dark, because their households have said they will not pay. The municipality says it can light all 40 km of roads from property tax, but the work will take a year. (a) Is a streetlight a public good? Give the reason from the chapter. (b) How much would the company collect each month? (c) Why does the company's plan leave the residential lanes dark? (d) Which plan, or mix of plans, fits the chapter's idea of a mixed economy? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Yes: a streetlight is available to everyone on the road, and one person's use does not stop others using it. (b) 120 x 300 = Rs 36,000 a month. (c) The company is a profit-making business; it lights only where shops will pay, and since no one can be kept from using a lit lane, it cannot charge the households who refuse to pay. (d) A mix fits best: the private company can light the market road now, earning its Rs 36,000, while the municipality lights the residential lanes from tax, since providing public goods is the government's role. In a mixed economy the government and private sector both play important roles. An answer choosing the municipality alone earns the mark if it argues that streetlights, as public goods, are the government's task.
s: (a) Yes, because it is available to all and one person's use does not prevent others
(b) Rs 36,000 a month
(c) Profit motive: it lights only where it can charge, and lane users cannot be made to pay
(d) A justified plan in which the government provides the public good, with or without the private firm
